extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, merchants, and readers of political economy / public finance
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for evaluating national monetary and trade policy — especially mercantilist/bullionist doctrines about accumulating gold and silver, balance of trade, and the financing of war. Draws on arguments and examples intended to guide governments and merchants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wealth consists in what money purchases, not in money
rubrics_metrics.description: Wealth does not consist in money, or in gold and silver; but in what money purchases, and is valuable only for purchasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Money makes part of national capital but is generally a small and the most unprofitable part. Policy should aim to increase the consumable goods and productive capital that money purchases, rather than to amass specie for its own sake. Anti-pattern: treating hoarded gold/silver as synonymous with national wealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Money is primarily a measure and instrument of value
rubrics_metrics.description: Because money is the measure of value, we estimate that of all other commodities by the quantity of money which they will exchange for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Money's primary role is to facilitate exchange and to be a common standard of value. Examples and idioms (a rich man is worth much money, etc.) illustrate its function. Policy evaluation should account for money's instrumentality rather than fetishizing its quantity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accumulating gold and silver by government is a misguided policy
rubrics_metrics.description: To attempt to increase the wealth of any country either by introducing or by detaining in it an unnecessary quantity of gold and silver is as absurd as obliging private families to keep unnecessary kitchen utensils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hoarding specie beyond its use diminishes resources available for consumption and production. Authorities attempting to increase wealth by detaining bullion will reduce real wealth that 'feeds, clothes, and lodges' the population.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibitions on bullion export are ineffective and counterproductive
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibitions could not hinder the exportation of gold and silver, which ... could easily be smuggled abroad; they only made it more dangerous and more expensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such prohibitions increase exchange costs, encourage smuggling, and do not stop bullion outflows. They distort exchange rates and may impose an effective tax raising the price of foreign goods. Historical practice (Spain, Portugal, old Scottish acts) shows limited usefulness and adverse effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of trade—not hoarding—determines bullion movements
rubrics_metrics.description: When the country exported to a greater value than it imported, a balance became due to it from foreign nations, which was necessarily paid to it in gold and silver; when it imported to a greater value than it exported, a contrary balance became due to foreign nations, which was necessarily paid to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bullion flows are the result of trade imbalances. Evaluations of monetary policy should focus on trade flows and exchanges rather than trying to directly manage specie totals. Mun’s framing (England’s Treasure in Foreign Trade) helped shape but also misdirected attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow free movement of foreign coin and bullion
rubrics_metrics.description: The prohibition of exporting gold and silver was, in France and England, confined to the coin of those respective countries. The exportation of foreign coin and of bullion was made free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical shift toward freeing foreign coin/bullion reflected merchants’ needs and demonstrated that restricting only local coin was inconsistent. Policy guidance: liberalize bullion/foreign coin flows rather than blanket bans on specie movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Home (inland) trade is the most important source of national prosperity
rubrics_metrics.description: The inland or home trade, the most important of all, ... was considered as subsidiary only to foreign trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Domestic trade, where equal capital affords greatest revenue and creates greatest employment, should not be treated as merely subsidiary to foreign trade. Policies prioritizing foreign trade over internal circulation risk neglecting the main engines of wealth and employment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity of money is regulated by effectual demand
rubrics_metrics.description: The quantity of every commodity which human industry can either purchase or produce, naturally regulates itself in every country according to the effectual demand...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Money supply adjusts to the demand for circulation. If additional coin is needed for increased circulation, it will be imported or created; if in excess, it will be exported. Policy should recognize market-driven adjustment rather than attempt heavy-handed control of specie quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Easy transport of bullion stabilizes its price (slow variation)
rubrics_metrics.description: On account of the small bulk and great value of those metals, no commodities can be more easily transported from one place to another ... the price of those metals does not fluctuate continually ... the changes to which it is liable are generally slow, gradual, and uniform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because bullion is easily moved, its price adjusts slowly and globally; only major shocks (e.g., discovery of America) cause rapid shifts. Policymakers should expect gradual adjustments rather than sudden speculative swings in specie value under normal conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complaints of money scarcity often reflect credit problems and over-trading
rubrics_metrics.description: No complaint ... is more common than that of a scarcity of money. ... Over-trading is the common cause of it. Many people wanted money who had nothing to give for them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shortages cited by merchants or towns may stem from imprudent expansion of trade relative to capital and credit constraints, not actual absence of gold/silver. Remedies should focus on credit, regulation of over-trading, and realistic project sizing rather than forcing specie inflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper money and credit can substitute for specie
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-regulated paper-money will supply it not only without any inconveniency, but, in some cases, with some advantages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In situations of specie shortfall, arrangements like buying and selling on credit, compensations among dealers, and well-managed paper instruments (exchequer notes, navy bills, bank bills) can effectively replace bullion in circulation. Proper regulation and confidence are key.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fleets and armies are maintained with consumable goods, not specie
rubrics_metrics.description: Fleets and armies are maintained, not with gold and silver, but with consumable goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National military expenditures are ultimately defrayed by the annual produce of land and labour and by exports of commodities rather than by hoarded treasure. Financing wars via exports, trade balances, and borrowing is historically more important than transferring specie.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish forms of accumulated specie and their wartime roles
rubrics_metrics.description: The gold and silver which can properly be considered as accumulated, or stored up in any country, may be distinguished into three parts; first, the circulating money; secondly, the plate of private families; and, last of all, the money which may have been collected by many years parsimony, and laid up in the treasury of the prince.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each category has different liquidity and usefulness in financing large expenditures. Circulating money is rarely redundant; private plate and princely treasure can be sources in extremis but are limited. Policy evaluation of wartime finance should account for these distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exporting bullion can be advantageous if it enables profitable commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: The exportation of gold and silver, in order to purchase foreign goods, might frequently increase the quantity [of bullion]; because, if the consumption of foreign goods was not thereby increased in the country, those goods might be re-exported ... being there sold for a large profit, might bring back much more treasure than was originally sent out to purchase them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat specie outflow as an investment: if exported to acquire goods that can be sold for profit elsewhere, the operation can increase national treasure. Policymakers should consider the broader commercial returns rather than judging bullion export as inherently harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government attention to preserving or augmenting money supply is generally unnecessary
rubrics_metrics.description: The attention of government never was so unnecessarily employed, as when directed to watch over the preservation or increase of the quantity of money in any country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because markets supply coin to meet effectual demand and credit substitutes exist, government efforts to micromanage specie totals are typically wasted and can be counterproductive. Public policy should focus on facilitating productive exchange and credit rather than policing bullion stocks.
